# Distributed communication and parameter residency

Sharding divides parameter or gradient storage among ranks. All-gather reconstructs complete values; reduce-scatter combines gradients and divides the result; replica reductions keep copies consistent. Scheduling or retaining storage can reduce waits but must preserve collective order and update semantics.

A **rank** is one training process, usually one GPU. A **collective** is a communication operation that every rank in a process group must call in the same order, such as all-reduce, all-gather or reduce-scatter. In fully sharded data parallel training (FSDP), each rank stores only a shard of each parameter, all-gathers the full parameter before a module uses it, frees the gathered copy afterward, and reduce-scatters gradients so each rank keeps the reduced gradient for its own shard.

[Model catalog](index.md)

**`accumulation_boundary_gradient_sync`: reduce gradients once per accumulated update**
- Trigger: Training already accumulates several microbatches per optimizer update, but redundantly reduces gradients after every microbatch. With `K` microbatches per update, this performs `K` gradient reductions although the update consumes only the reduction of the accumulated sum.
- Technique: Suppress gradient synchronization for non-final microbatches and reduce the complete accumulated gradient on the final one. For DDP, the synchronization-suppression context must cover both forward and backward of each non-final microbatch. Keep the existing effective batch and update schedule unchanged.
- Guards: Preserve loss weighting, accumulation boundaries, clipping, overflow handling and scheduler/checkpoint counters. Coordinate skipped or partial batches across ranks; never update unreduced local gradients. Test conditional and unused parameters and framework-version restrictions. FSDP may retain full-size gradients while synchronization is deferred. Validate moments, quality and native resume; do not conflate this with increasing batch size.
- Reference: [DDP `no_sync`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.15/generated/torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel.html). Cover both forward and backward for non-final microbatches; the next normal pass performs synchronization. Other sharding runtimes have different memory and synchronization contracts.

**`bounded_parameter_allgather_prefetch`: start parameter all-gathers ahead of use, within a bound**
- Trigger: Computation waits for sharded parameters to be gathered even though preceding modules or pipeline stages provide useful overlap time. If each module issues its all-gather only when it starts, the GPU computes nothing during that communication.
- Technique: Issue upcoming parameter all-gathers during preceding independent compute and wait only at first use. Bound the lookahead and in-flight bytes, because every prefetched parameter occupies full-size memory until it is used and freed. In pipelines, tune prefetch distance independently of the residency/eviction window so staggering communication does not add re-gathers. FSDP-style runtimes expose explicit forward and backward prefetch controls, such as `set_modules_to_forward_prefetch` and `set_modules_to_backward_prefetch`; check what the installed version supports.
- Guards: Derive the real execution order, including checkpoint replay and repeated microbatches; do not assume backward is always reverse forward. Preserve collective order and group membership across ranks. Handle unused prefetches and retained buffers safely; ignore unsharded/skipped modules. Check all-rank peak memory, real communication traces, gradient/quality and resume parity. This mechanism does not itself hide reduce-scatter. A schedule checked only with stand-in collectives is still a proposal: verify overlap and correctness in traces of the actual communication, not just scheduling tests.

**`forward_backward_parameter_residency`: keep gathered parameters from forward for backward**
- Trigger: Forward gathers parameters, immediately discards the gathered copy, and backward gathers the same unchanged parameters again despite memory headroom. The second all-gather moves the same bytes again only because the first copy was freed.
- Technique: Keep selected gathered parameter groups resident across the forward-to-backward interval, removing their backward re-gather instead of merely prefetching it. Retain gradient sharding and normal optimizer ownership. In FSDP-style runtimes this corresponds to not resharding selected modules after forward, for example `reshard_after_forward=False`; check the installed version's option.
- Guards: Budget overlapping parameter residency with activations, gradients and other microbatches on every rank. Verify the setting reaches the live sharding implementation and that the collective actually disappears. Check pipeline/offload compatibility, parameter freshness and checkpoint semantics. Measure interactions with other communicator traffic; validate gradients, quality and resume before accepting the tradeoff. Sharing a communicator with other traffic regressed in one tested case, and favorable comparisons across differently configured runs were confounded; compare this choice against a baseline on the same workload and configuration.

**`overlap_aware_collective_bucketing`: bucket small collectives without losing overlap**
- Trigger: Many small collectives pay launch latency, but indiscriminate coalescing delays early-ready results and destroys existing compute overlap. During backward, gradients for later layers become ready first. A large bucket cannot start communicating until every gradient in it is ready, so its communication starts late and has less backward computation left to overlap with.
- Technique: Bucket compatible, dependency-ready collectives only when saved launch latency outweighs lost overlap. Favor exposed communication, keep early critical-path buckets small, and cap buffer/in-flight memory. DDP's `bucket_cap_mb` is one existing control over bucket size.
- Guards: Match process group, reduction operation, dtype, parameter order, sizes and normalization on every rank, including unused-gradient cases. Preserve buffer lifetimes, waits and cross-stream control dependencies. Synchronize profile-derived scheduling decisions across ranks. Verify actual message counts, all-rank memory, numerical/quality and resume parity; fewer collectives alone is not an acceptance test.

**`topology_tiered_hybrid_sharding`: shard within fast topology tiers and replicate across slow ones**
- Trigger: Full-world parameter gathers/reductions cross slow network tiers and become exposed as the training rank count grows. When every rank holds a shard of every parameter, each all-gather and reduce-scatter spans all ranks, so its traffic crosses the slowest links, such as those between hosts, on every step.
- Technique: Form smaller topology-local shard groups for parameter all-gather and gradient reduce-scatter. Replicate those shard groups and synchronize corresponding gradient shards across the replica dimension, so slow-tier links carry sharded rather than full-parameter traffic. For example, shard within each host's fast interconnect and replicate across hosts; FSDP-style runtimes call this hybrid sharding and configure it with a two-dimensional device mesh or hybrid sharding strategy.
- Guards: Map logical groups to actual network topology and keep the mesh identical across ranks. Account for increased parameter/optimizer replication memory. Apply shard and replica reductions with correct global sample normalization, without double reduction: the combined scaling must match the original global normalization, for example dividing by the shard-group size in one reduction and by the replica count in the other rather than by the full world size in both. Preserve logical parameter/optimizer identities across checkpoint resharding. Validate gradients, quality and resumed runs on the real topology.
